Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so. Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment. Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said. The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts. A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy." TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime. Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups. In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time. Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those [USN:S0N3ON011 TEXT:"announced against Mexican cartels"] in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said. Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees. The State Department announced the designation the following day. Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision. BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro. Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil. Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said. Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS (JBSS.O) - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down. Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March [USN:S0N3ZG01R TEXT:"Brazil barred Beattie"] from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison. Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity. Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory. "Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually."

item.title: Lindt got chocolate price hikes wrong, chairman says after CEO's ouster
item.description: Lindt & Sprüngli misjudged how consumers would respond to price increases, the chair of the Swiss chocolate maker said, days after the company ousted its CEO.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Lindt & Sprüngli (LISN.S) has struggled because it misjudged how consumers would respond to price increases, the chair of the Swiss chocolate maker said, days after the company [USN:L6N4650EX TEXT:"ousted"] its CEO over concerns about its performance. In an interview with the NZZ am Sonntag newspaper, Executive Chairman Ernst Tanner said the firm, whose shares have tumbled more than 25% this year after recent outlook [USN:L8N45L05W TEXT:"cuts"], was largely suffering because it had misread the market in Germany. "We misjudged how customers would respond to price increases. After cocoa prices reached historic highs from 2024 onwards, we wanted to pass on those additional costs. In doing so, we overestimated how much we could raise prices without hurting demand," he said. "For some consumers, our products clearly became too expensive in recent months." "Lindt & Sprüngli as a whole, however, is not in crisis," Tanner added, arguing the company's shares are now undervalued. "In the Americas and the Far East, we'll achieve our growth targets of 6% to 8% this year as well." Tanner, 80, who was CEO from 1993 to 2016 and has been chairman for over three decades, rejected the suggestion that he should stand down, saying he had important work to do to get Lindt back on track. "Once that's been achieved, I look forward to turning to the next phase of my life," he said. Tanner said the company had already cut some prices as it seeks to lift sales volumes, and would have more scope to do so once cocoa prices returned to more normal levels. He said there would not be group-wide job cuts and that the firm wanted to keep growing. Still, he said thrift was required and that bonuses would be affected in the Germany-Switzerland-Austria region as targets had been missed.

item.title: Trump announces Audi will build $4 billion US factory in Georgia
item.description: Trump's tariffs dealt Audi a $1.4 billion blow last year.
item.dc:creator: Bo Erickson, David Shepardson
item.content:encoded: US President Donald Trump announced on Saturday that Audi plans to build a $4 billion assembly plant in Georgia that will produce 200,000 SUVs annually, as he seeks to convince Americans to back Republicans in the November midterm elections. Trump, who has pressured automakers to move production to the United States and has raised tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum and parts, made the announcement at a rally in Perry, near Macon in central Georgia, where Volkswagen's premium subsidiary intends to build its first US assembly plant. Last year, Trump's tariffs dealt Audi a €1.2 billion ($1.4 billion) blow as it imports all its vehicles for the US market from Europe or Mexico. Georgia has competitive election races for US Senate and governor and Trump is eager to make the case that his auto tariffs are helping the US economy. Critics say they have boosted vehicle prices and that the trade uncertainty has delayed some automaker investments. "We are planning to bring our biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia," Audi CEO Gernot Doellner said at the event. "This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market." In Germany, meanwhile, there has been [USN:L8N4690LO TEXT:"increasing tension"] between Volkswagen management and workers over massive job cuts in the carmaker's home market, including possible plant closures in light of rising costs and stiff Asian competition. "It is right and necessary to better tap into the US market via a new plant," said Christiane Benner, head of the IG Metall union and Volkswagen's deputy supervisory board chair. "However, firm prospects for workers at all sites, particularly those here in Germany, must be clearly defined and set out." She said a final decision on the investment would have to be taken by Volkswagen's supervisory board. Olaf Lies, state premier of the German state of Lower Saxony, Volkswagen's second-largest shareholder, said that expanded production in the US was an opportunity provided German workers also benefit. "Growth in America must secure jobs and value creation here and must not displace them," he said. REPUBLICAN SAYS TARIFFS BROUGHT AUDI PLANT TO UNITED STATES Audi said the investment will create approximately 4,500 jobs. Construction is scheduled to begin next year, with production starting in the early 2030s, Audi said. The plant is expected to assemble the Audi Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, a US official told Reuters. Audi also plans to build 25,000 vehicles a year in neighboring South Carolina, the official said. Some of the vehicles, now built in Europe, would be exported, the official added. Those vehicles will be assembled at a $2 billion plant of VW's off-road brand Scout Motors that is under construction in Blythewood, near the state capital, Columbia, the official said. "We regard the region as a key market for profitable growth," Volkswagen CEO Oliver Blume said. "A potential Audi plant in the US would create further conditions for this." Trump has cut government incentives for electric vehicles, causing a significant reduction in EV and battery production in the country. US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year. A gold Audi with manufacturer license plates was parked outside Trump's rally. US Senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, said late on Saturday that "with this investment, Audi will build all of their SUVs exclusively in the US". He said the Audi plant "would never have happened without tariffs, without common sense regulations and without eliminating California’s ability to regulate fuel economy standards". Audi sales have fallen for two consecutive years and slid 7% in the first half of 2026 as fierce competition in China and US tariffs hit demand. Audi's US sales are down 16% this year. Audi's Neckarsulm plant in southwest Germany is one of four German Volkswagen plants facing possible closure after 2030. In July, Japan's Toyota (7203.T) said it would spend $3.6 billion to build a 2.5 million square foot (232,000 square metre) truck assembly line on its manufacturing campus in San Antonio, Texas, and shift some truck production to the US from Mexico. The Japanese automaker said the expansion would be completed by 2030, creating 2,000 jobs. Honda Motor (7267.T) is considering building a US assembly plant but has warned it may not unless the US-Mexico-Canada Agreement on trade is extended. South Korea's Hyundai said last year that if it had certainty about USMCA, it "would immediately unlock over $20 billion in new American investments".

item.title: Tristan Luneau pushes Ducks past resurgent Flyers
item.description: Tristan Luneau had a goal and two assists as the visiting Anaheim Ducks snapped a five-game losing streak with a 5-4 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Tristan Luneau had a goal and two assists as the visiting Anaheim Ducks snapped a five-game losing streak with a 5-4 victory over the Philadelphia Flyers on Saturday. Leo Carlsson chipped in with a goal and an assist against the team that signed him to a five-year, $90 million offer sheet over the summer. Anaheim ultimately matched the deal, making the 21-year-old the highest paid player in the league. Matvei Michkov scored his seventh and eighth goals for Philadelphia, which had won three straight since losing its first nine contests. Porter Martone had a goal and an assist and Tyson Foerster also scored for the Flyers, while Trevor Zegras recorded two assists against his former team. The Ducks took a 5-3 lead with two goals early in the third period. The go-ahead tally was Luneau's first of the season on a seemingly harmless shot that snuck past Joseph Woll two minutes into the period. Beckett Sennecke then created a two-goal lead when he tipped home a feed from Carlsson for a power-play goal at 7:10. Just over a minute later, Michkov poked in a loose puck to bring the Flyers within 5-4. Philadelphia never seriously threatened down the stretch, despite getting a power play for the final 40.7 seconds. Anaheim's Sam Colangelo and A.J. Greer took simultaneous minor penalties with 6:19 left in the first period -- a sequence that led to two Philadelphia goals. Michkov scored first on a shot through traffic with the Flyers skating 5-on-3 at 13:59, and then Martone scored on a great setup from Travis Sanheim on the ensuing 5-on-4 at 15:02. The Ducks got on the board midway through the second period, as Cutter Gauthier stole the puck behind the net and found Carlsson for a goal. Greer tied it less than five minutes later, but the Flyers answered right back. Foerster gave the hosts a 3-2 lead with a short-handed goal against Lukas Dostal at 15:04. But the visitors responded just over a minute later as Judd Caulfield tipped in a centering pass by Alex Killorn to create a 3-3 tie. Anaheim received a power play late in the second period, but Woll held firm with back-to-back terrific saves against Gauthier. Woll finished with 21 saves for the Flyers, while Dostal turned aside 28 shots for the Ducks. --Field Level Media

item.title: Protests sweep Italian cities amid heavy security presence, some violence reported
item.description: Authorities deployed a heavy police presence and many shops closed as a precaution.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Protests against war and rising living costs took place in major Italian cities on Saturday, with some incidents of violence, a week after unrest erupted across the country. Authorities deployed a heavy police presence and many shops closed as a precaution against possible damage. The demonstrations, [USN:L8N4650S6 TEXT:"which followed clashes last weekend"] in which protesters fought with police, looted shops and vandalised property, were violent in Turin, Rome and Bologna, with clashes between officers and demonstrators. They were largely peaceful in Milan. Reuters witnesses did not observe any shops being looted or property vandalised. After calls for further demonstrations circulated on social media this week, authorities made extensive security arrangements and deployed large numbers of police officers to prevent a repeat of last weekend's violence. Earlier on Saturday, Italian police said they had detained a person allegedly linked to organising the "October 17 Movement" — last weekend's protests — and had taken them to police headquarters in Milan for questioning.

item.title: Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, intelligence memo warns
item.description: The alert came after Washington scaled back staffing at its mission in Saudi Arabia earlier this week.
item.dc:creator: Humeyra Pamuk, Enas Alashray
item.content:encoded: Iran has ramped up efforts to target US personnel, and lethal plots by Tehran against American citizens have reached "advanced stages", a senior intelligence official in the Trump administration warned in a memo seen by Reuters. The alert from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton came after Washington scaled back staffing at its mission in Saudi Arabia earlier this week in response to intensified attacks by Iran-allied Houthi forces. Those attacks on one front of the nearly eight-month-old regional conflict triggered by the Iran war have coincided with [USN:L8N4682UH TEXT:"a rise in attacks"] on commercial shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Earlier this month, sources told Reuters Iran was preparing a [USN:L8N45M1N4 TEXT:"more forceful response"] if the United States resumes large-scale military attacks on its territory. "Specifically, through various channels, we have received intelligence that Iran has substantially increased efforts to target US personnel," Clayton wrote to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in a message dated October 23. "The lethal plotting efforts by the Iranians against US citizens have reached advanced stages in both the Middle East and certain other countries," he added. CIA Director John Ratcliffe was also copied in on the unclassified memo which was first reported by Axios. The State Department on Wednesday [USN:L6N46718Z TEXT:"ordered"] non-emergency government employees and their family members to leave US diplomatic missions in Saudi Arabia and planned to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the region, US officials told Reuters. On Saturday, the US State Department updated travel advisories for more than a dozen countries across the Gulf and Middle East, including Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Israel, citing an increased threat from Iran-aligned Houthis. "When it comes to our staffing at embassies, we constantly evaluate new information about the security environment," a US official said. "The threat of Houthi attacks and of Iranian terror plots targeting US officials are informing our decisions on staffing adjustments for embassies on RO Status in the region," the official said. The Restricted Operations Status provides the State Department more flexibility in personnel decisions without having to publicly announce a change in the status of a mission. The Iran war is a week away from entering its ninth month and has significantly weighed on the approval ratings of US President Donald Trump ahead of midterm elections on November 3.

item.title: UAE's Ras Al Khaimah shuts all beaches as neighbours grapple with oil spill
item.description: Residents reported unusual odours in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE's environment ministry said they posed no health risks.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Ras Al Khaimah authorities said on Saturday that all beaches in the emirate would be closed until further notice, a day after an offshore oil leak prompted beach closures in neighbouring Umm Al Quwain and Sharjah. The Public Services Department announced the closures in a statement shared by Ras Al Khaimah Police General Headquarters. No reason was given. The United Arab Emirates [USN:L1N469029 TEXT:"said on Friday"] that efforts were underway to contain oil leaking from a tanker offshore, with its Ministry of Climate Change and Environment conducting an environmental assessment. All beaches and coastal areas around the city of Umm Al Quwain were temporarily closed until technical teams completed their assessments and determined the necessary safety and marine protection measures, the ministry said. The ministry also urged fishermen and other sea users to avoid affected areas and follow official instructions. Authorities in Sharjah temporarily closed Al Hamriyah Beach, on the UAE's northern coast near the border with Umm Al Quwain, as a precaution, the Sharjah Government Media Bureau said. Since the start of the US-Israeli war with Iran , attacks on commercial vessels in Gulf shipping lanes have heightened concerns about maritime security and the conflict's environmental fallout. Ras Al Khaimah, a northern UAE emirate known for its beaches and luxury resorts, is also home to Wynn Resorts' planned casino resort on Al Marjan Island. The Las Vegas-based operator, which won the UAE's first commercial gaming licence in 2024, said in February it expected the resort to open in the first quarter of 2027. Wynn said in March [USN:L4N44122B TEXT:"it had resumed"] construction after a brief pause, even as the Iran war continued to disrupt businesses across the Middle East. Residents reported unusual odours in parts of Sharjah, Ajman and Umm Al Quwain, but the UAE's environment ministry said they posed no health risks. The smell remained pungent across Umm Al Quwain on Friday. UAE authorities have not named the tanker involved in the incident or said what caused the spill.

item.title: Around 1,200 Palestinians are displaced in Hebron as Israel begins military operation
item.description: The Palestinian Authority criticised the operation as a "collective punishment."
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Israeli military forced around 1,200 Palestinians to leave their homes in Hebron in the occupied West Bank, a Palestinian official said on Saturday, a day after a Palestinian attack [USN:L1N4690KO TEXT:"killed two Israeli"] soldiers. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday had said the military would launch a large-scale operation after the soldiers were killed when two Palestinian gunmen opened fire at a military checkpoint near the city. The Israeli military said the gunmen were shot dead. They also said the operation in the Al-Jaladah and Ein Deir Baha neighbourhoods near the military checkpoint at the entrance of Hebron was to search for militants and weapons. In a statement, it also said the military would carry out demolitions. The Palestinian Authority criticised the operation as a "collective punishment". Yousef Zouhair Al-Jabari, the head of Hebron's municipality, said around 1,300 faced losing their homes in addition to the 1,200 already displaced. He also said the Israeli operations were motivated by parliamentary elections on Tuesday when Netanyahu's right-wing coalition may lose his majority, opinion polls show. "Netanyahu and the radical ministers in his government are trying to win as many votes as possible from the settlers," Al-Jabari said. The non-governmental organisation the Palestinian Prisoners' Club said Israeli forces had arrested around 70 Palestinians on Friday and Saturday. Israeli officials have not commented on any arrests. NETANYAHU'S GOVERNMENT HAS PRESIDED OVER EXPANSION OF SETTLEMENTS Al-Jabari said the military had demolished shops, factories, homes, and roads in Hebron and that the response was disproportionate and unjustified. Residents in Hebron told Reuters that the military expelled many people with no connection to the Palestinian attackers. "We are calling on officials to stand by us because we are not involved in any of this. There are children. We are isolated; we don’t do anything. This is all arbitrary,” said Majdi Nasser, one of those driven from his home. Residents told Reuters they saw Israeli soldiers marking homes with a black X after their Palestinian occupants had been forced to leave. It was not immediately clear what the X mark meant. Netanyahu's government has presided over a rapid [USN:L6N44Y077 TEXT:"expansion"] of settlements, deemed illegal by UN bodies and most countries, though Israel disputes this. Across the West Bank, Israel has blocked the entrances to most Palestinian cities and towns, severely curtailing Palestinians' freedom of movement. Yousef Mur, a resident of the Palestinian town of Yatta, said the closures meant he was unable to reach Jerusalem with his daughter for her cancer treatment. "The situation is bad, and we are suffering. When we tried to cross, they fired stun grenades towards us, and my girl got scared on the way. They fired stun grenades towards people. The situation is very difficult," Mur said. (This story has been refiled to remove the repeated word 'when' in paragraph 2.)

item.title: Five takeaways from Trump's midterm campaign rallies
item.description: Trump boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and admires a Republican’s buttocks.
item.dc:creator: Steve Holland, Bo Erickson, Nandita Bose, Jacob Bogage
item.content:encoded: President Donald Trump is in the midst of a nationwide campaign blitz ahead of the November midterm elections, holding near-daily rallies to boost turnout for Republicans who are fighting to keep control of Congress. In his 90-minute stump speeches, Trump defends his economic policies, boasts about crowd size, mocks protesters and has even admired a fellow Republican’s buttocks. Here are five takeaways from Reuters coverage of the president’s appearances, staged mostly in Republican-friendly areas across the country: TRUMP'S ECONOMIC PITCH COLLIDES WITH VOTER REALITY At the start of the month, Trump said he had done a “[USN:L1N45M10K TEXT:"bad job"]” explaining his economic record. He has tried to remedy that at his rallies, pointing to a record-low [USN:S0N4310A5 TEXT:"poverty rate"], low [USN:L1N45N170 TEXT:"unemployment,"] record highs in the [USN:L6N45S0IV TEXT:"stock market"] and cheaper prices for some food items. But his sales pitch is colliding with voters' concerns about how much they are spending on gas, groceries and other everyday expenses. Consumer prices accelerated in September as the cost of gasoline surged. The nationwide average price of gas is $4.27 per gallon ($1.13 per litre), nearly 40% higher than a year ago, according to AAA. Trump has repeatedly promised that gas prices will fall once the Iran war ends. The disconnect was evident outside Trump's rally in rural Kansas, where Chester Daniel, a 90-year-old military veteran and Trump supporter, said the economy has “a long way to go” to help working people. “Prices? Too high! We will never go back to what they were when this all started, but they need to come way down," Daniel said. "I don’t know how these young people make a living for their family." RALLY MAP SHOWS REPUBLICANS PLAYING DEFENSE Trump's travel map signals just how difficult it will be for Republicans to retain control of Congress, with the president forced to play defense deep in conservative territory. Trump has traveled twice to Texas for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton, campaigned for Republican Senate incumbent Roger Marshall in Kansas and made two stops in Ohio for Senator Jon Husted. Trump also rallied for Republicans in competitive races in Alaska, Iowa, Montana and South Carolina. He is set to visit Mississippi on Monday. Those are places Republicans are accustomed to winning easily, not battlegrounds where Trump would spend time during the crucial final weeks before an election. Paxton narrowly trails Democrat James Talarico in polls, while Marshall faces a serious challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton in a state that has not elected a Democratic senator in nearly a century. Husted trails former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown in polls in Ohio, and Republican Senate hopeful Ashley Hinson is in a close race against Democrat Josh Turek in Iowa. Notably absent from Trump's travels so far with less than two weeks until Election Day: Michigan, Maine, Minnesota and New Hampshire – also home to tight Senate races. He is soon poised to hit some of those locations. He is scheduled travel to Michigan on Sunday and has said he also plans to go to Maine. TRUMP'S BOASTS ABOUT BIG CROWDS MEET UNEVEN REALITY Trump has made crowd sizes a recurring theme of his midterm rallies, portraying packed arenas and thousands of people he says are stranded outside as evidence of his persisting popularity. But actual turnout on the campaign trail in recent weeks has been uneven. Some rallies have drawn capacity crowds but have shown little sign of the overflow Trump described. At others, large sections of seats remained empty even in modest-sized venues. "I'm doing these every night, and no matter where I go, it's the same thing. It's massive crowds," Trump said at a rally in North Carolina on Tuesday. "We have big screens outside. Thousands and thousands of people. There's something going on that's very special." The venue was filled to capacity, but there were no signs of crowds outside waiting to get in or watching on screens. At an October 7 rally in San Antonio, Texas, Trump said lines stretched two miles outside the arena even as sizable sections inside remained empty. Crowd sizes are not always an accurate measure of political support, but Trump has pointed to them as a sign of strength even as his approval rating has fallen to 31%, the lowest of either of his presidential terms, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll released on Monday. Trump is not on the ballot on November 3. For Republican candidates, the question is whether the enthusiasm he generates among his supporters can translate into votes for them. FRANCE BECOMES A 'BETE NOIRE' FOR MIDTERMS Trump has often used French President Emmanuel Macron as a foil in his campaign stump speeches, claiming he strong-armed Macron into raising prescription drug prices in France by threatening tariffs on a popular French export, champagne, and other goods. But in the last week or so Trump has seized on another narrative about France, casting its violent unrest of recent weeks as a warning of what he says could happen in the US if Democrats win in the midterms. Trump has blamed the unrest on migrants and Muslims, following a familiar playbook that has featured in his politics for more than a decade. “What the hell happened to France?” Trump told a crowd in a livestock competition arena in Clemson, South Carolina, on Wednesday. Notably, the French protests have taken a larger role in Trump’s recent speeches than two other major foreign policy headaches he has been unable to resolve: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and his war against Iran. “They’ll end one way or another,” Trump said of the two conflicts at his Clemson rally. He did not elaborate on how they might end, but complained that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for his work to resolve conflicts around the world. TRUMP PUTS THE BODY IN BODY POLITIC Trump has long had a fixation on the human physique that stretches beyond the body politic. This campaign season, Trump has given particular attention to Husted, a 59-year-old former college football player for the University of Dayton. At rallies in Ohio, Kentucky and North Carolina, Trump marveled at Husted’s physique, at one point saying his backside is “like a pile of muscle.” “Then I looked at his legs, and I said, ‘Man, his feet are big.’ Then I looked at his shoulders, and I tapped him on the shoulder, and it actually hurt my hand. It was like a piece of steel. I said, ‘This guy’s a monster,’” Trump said. Trump had similar praise on Friday for Robert F. Kennedy Jr., his secretary of health and human services, telling a campaign rally in Florida that the 72-year-old "has the body of a 30-year-old." Such riffs are familiar terrain for Trump. At the close of his 2024 campaign, he used a Pennsylvania rally speech to tell a crude story about PGA legend Arnold Palmer's prowess beyond his golf game. Trump's focus over the years on people's physical attributes has also included mocking the weight and looks of his opponents. Trump finds even some of his friends lacking in fashion sense, including the rumpled Paxton. "Some may not like the way he dresses," Trump said about him at the Republicans' midterm convention in Dallas in mid-September, adding: "I don't." That has not stopped Trump from campaigning for Paxton, however. He returns to Texas on Tuesday for two more campaign rallies.

item.title: Violence flares in Paris after largely peaceful protests across France
item.description: Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers boarding up storefronts and museums closing their doors.
item.dc:creator: Juliette Jabkhiro, Yann Tessier, Crispian Balmer
item.content:encoded: Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators marched in France on Saturday, with largely peaceful rallies giving way to clashes in Paris and Marseille as night fell despite a huge security operation aimed at preventing a repeat of [USN:L1N46608H TEXT:"last week's unrest"]. The Interior Ministry said 410,000 people took part in protests nationwide, though unions said the true figure was twice as high. The main demonstration took place on the southeastern fringes of Paris, where at least 110,000 people turned out to denounce rising living costs and growing inequality. The atmosphere deteriorated sharply after the rally ended. Riot police fired tear gas and water cannon at a group of around 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed on a cold, rainy evening. In France's second city, Marseille, youths set fire to rubbish bins to block roads, and hurled rocks and bottles at security forces. Police said several stores, including two jewellery shops, were ransacked. Clashes also flared in Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse. "In almost every march we saw the formation of these high-risk groups. They broke away from the main body and sought to commit acts of violence," said Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, accusing far-left activists and criminal gangs of seeking to foment trouble. PARIS IN LOCKDOWN Authorities deployed 70,000 police officers and gendarmes, 10,000 more than a week earlier, after conceding they had underestimated the scale of the unrest on October 17. Nunez told reporters the violence was less intense than a week ago, when looters and vandals went on the rampage. "What changed was anticipation," he said. He also said far-right activists had sought confrontations with leftist groups in the southern cities of Nice and Montpellier, opening a potential new front in the disturbances. Much of central Paris took on the appearance of a city under lockdown, with shopkeepers [USN:L2N46A00I TEXT:"boarding up storefronts"], [USN:L5N46A022 TEXT:"museums closing their doors"] and more than 20 metro stations shut. Business groups urged retailers to remain closed after thousands of shops and businesses were damaged or looted across France last weekend. "There are hardly any customers, so it's not really worth staying open," said Oskar, manager of a Kiton boutique in Paris. Several of the capital's best-known cultural institutions, including the Louvre, the Musee d'Orsay and the Paris Opera, closed for the day as a precaution, leaving tourists frustrated. "Everything's boarded up and we're not quite sure where we should be," said Xavier Dolliole, a tourist from the US city of New Orleans. PROTESTS RIPPLE ACROSS EUROPE The nationwide disorder began with small student demonstrations in suburban Paris last month to denounce school conditions. It swiftly broadened into a wider protest against the government's economic policies and inspired demonstrations in neighbouring countries. On Saturday [USN:L6N46A05C TEXT:"Belgian police"] used tear gas and pepper spray as they clashed in Brussels with anti-government demonstrators, with protests also taking place in a number of Italian cities for a second weekend, [USN:L2N46A02Y TEXT:"and in Albania"]. Hard-left leader Jean-Luc Melenchon, who joined the Paris rally, predicted the protests would continue until President Emmanuel Macron, whose mandate expires next year, addressed the social malaise in France, one of the world's richest nations. "Given the current situation, I think he will come to understand that this will happen again every week. There is still time for (Macron) to give in. After that, the only thing left to him will be the exit door," Melenchon told reporters. FAR-RIGHT PARTY HOLDS CONGRESS Many demonstrators accused the government of overreacting to last week's turmoil, as soldiers were dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees, a grand boulevard lined with luxury shops and restaurants. "We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student. "My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added. The first authorised march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally, which is holding a party congress in the city. A [USN:L6N4690NC TEXT:"shooting"] west of Paris on Friday heightened tensions. A gunman suspected of acting out of Islamophobic hatred killed one person and wounded four others, including a 12-year-old girl. "We have come to tell the far right, face-to-face, that we are not afraid," said Bally Bagayoko, the mayor of Saint-Denis and a member of Melenchon's France Unbowed party.

item.title: Wall St Week Ahead Earnings flood, Fed meeting will test rickety AI market rally
item.description: US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a Federal Reserve meeting posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally.
item.dc:creator: Lewis Krauskopf
item.content:encoded: US stock investors face a pivotal week, with corporate earnings reports led by major AI players and a Federal Reserve meeting posing critical tests for a suddenly shaky market rally. Weakness in technology shares left investors [USN:L6N468196 TEXT:"on edge about the state of the AI trade"] that has driven the US equity bull market that just marked its fourth anniversary. The Nasdaq Composite (.IXIC) posted a slim loss on Friday, a day after the tech-heavy index suffered its biggest daily drop since June. Investors were disappointed by quarterly reports from Meta (META.O) and Lam Research (LRCX.O) . Meta is one of the hyperscalers spending massively to build out data centers, while Lam is a high-flying semiconductor company, one of a group that has been among the biggest AI stock winners. Three other hyperscalers -- Alphabet (GOOGL.O) , Microsoft (MSFT.O) and Amazon (AMZN.O) -- headline a packed week of quarterly results, including about one-third of S&P 500 companies. The Fed's interest rate policy meeting on Wednesday also could rattle markets. "There are a lot of balls in the air," said Nick Giorgi, chief equity strategist at Alpine Macro. "Next week, you have a lot more tech earnings, and right now the market is taking a discerning eye as it relates to all the spending that goes along with artificial intelligence," Giorgi said. "The market's just not giving the benefit of the doubt to companies that are spending a ton of money on building this all out, which to us is actually very healthy, but still does augur for some short-term pain." Investors also have their focus trained on the US midterm elections on November 3, with growing bets that the Democrats will wrest control of the US Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party. The series of market catalysts could ratchet up volatility over the next couple of weeks and challenge optimism that has helped lift the benchmark S&P 500 index (.SPX) up 11% in 2026. HYPERSCALERS ON THE HOT SEAT Robust US profit growth has underpinned the stock market's gains this year in the face of headwinds including spiking Treasury yields and rising energy costs stemming from the Middle East conflict. With more than 100 companies having posted results so far, third-quarter S&P 500 earnings are on pace to have climbed more than 32% from a year ago, according to LSEG IBES data. Next week is the busiest of the reporting season. "I think earnings will determine whether this ... tech pullback is a buying opportunity, or is there a deeper correction ahead," said King Lip, chief strategist at BakerAvenue Wealth Management. "What we need is just another round of really strong earnings." Alphabet and Microsoft report on Wednesday. Amazon's results are due Thursday. Focus will be on the guidance the companies give on capital spending plans and whether they are seeing returns on the massive outlays. Capital spending from hyperscalers, expected to be around $800 billion this year, is boosting the bottom lines for a wide swath of companies involved in the AI buildout. But investors are wary of the sustainability of such spending amid mounting financing costs. "Earnings are critical to the overall confidence level of the AI trade and how much longer the spend will continue," said Kevin Mahn, president and chief investment officer at Hennion & Walsh Asset Management. FED EXPECTED TO PAUSE ON RATES, FOR NOW Quarterly reports next week from chip companies Intel (INTC.O) and Sandisk (SNDK.O) also could influence the AI trade. Elsewhere, other high-profile companies set to report next week include drugmaker Eli Lilly (LLY.N) , oil majors Exxon (XOM.N) and Chevron (CVX.N) and industrial equipment giant Caterpillar (CAT.N) . The prospect for more interest rate hikes also comes into focus with the Fed meeting. The Fed raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, in an effort to control above-target inflation, but Fed funds futures late on Friday suggested a less-than 10% chance the Fed will hike again when it gives its policy statement on Wednesday, according to LSEG data. One factor: Investors are dubious that the Fed will want to increase rates just a week before the midterm elections. However, markets are leaning toward a hike at the next meeting in December, with futures suggesting a roughly 80% probability of such a move then. Walter Todd, chief investment officer at Greenwood Capital, said he will be watching for any hints about the rate path at Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's press conference following the decision. "Does he say something to give an idea about December, because right now the expectation is there is going to be a hike," Todd said.

item.title: Ozempic wave boosts US cobblers and tailors as Americans tighten their belts
item.description: Read more in our series about weight-loss drugs and how they are changing our habits.
item.dc:creator: Danielle Kaye, Alexander Marrow
item.content:encoded: Lorraine Scott has spent at least $300 to tailor her pants and jeans since losing 60 pounds on weight-loss drugs over the past year. This is the fourth story in a five-part Reuters series on how weight-loss drugs are changing the way people shop and eat, and how companies are responding to the trend. "Most of the things in my closet didn't fit anymore," she said. The 42-year-old Atlanta resident, who is known as Lorraine Kamesha to her YouTube followers, has opted to alter her favorite pairs of pants instead of investing in new ones as her weight fluctuates, while turning to fast fashion for the rest of her wardrobe. US consumers taking weight-loss drugs like Novo Nordisk's Ozempic and Eli Lilly's Mounjaro have turned to cobblers and tailors as they try to save money while shedding pounds, motivated in part by a cost-of-living squeeze and rising out-of-pocket costs for the drugs as US employers [USN:L1N44L0V0 TEXT:"increasingly drop GLP-1 coverage"]. Over the past year, leather repairers have seen a spike in requests for their services due to rapid weight loss — not just for belts, but also for shoe and bag strap adjustments tailored to customers' trimmer bodies. The uptick in demand for alterations underscores how weight-loss drugs are upending the retail sector, with some corners of the industry well-positioned to benefit while others struggle to adapt. About 11% of US adults are on GLP-1 drugs to lose weight, according to Gallup, forcing millions of consumers to look for affordable ways to [USN:L6N43B0UY TEXT:"revamp their wardrobes"]. Cobblers Direct, an online shoe and handbag repair shop with 25 brick-and-mortar stores in Texas and a nationwide mail-in service, is seeing double-digit year-on-year growth in its belt-shortening business, said CEO Stephen Kelly. The company, whose around 100 artisans will soon be operating from a new, nearly 30,000-square-foot warehouse in Austin, is now shortening as much as 500 belts each week, Kelly said. Customers, he said, have been walking into the stores with five or six belts slung across their shoulder. After getting a few more holes punched in, some have asked to keep the extra flap of leather as a "badge of honor." "They'll pull their belt out and show how long their belt originally was. And then they tuck it back into their waistline," Kelly said. About 80% of GLP-1 users are living in clothes that no longer fit, waiting six months on average before buying anything new, according to a survey of more than 700 US adults using weight-loss drugs by telehealth platform Trimi. Jeans are the most disrupted article of clothing, the survey found, with 90% of users lamenting poor fit. After going off weight-loss drugs, people regain on average 60% of their lost weight within a year, researchers at the University of Cambridge found this year, adding to users' reluctance to go all-in on an entirely new wardrobe. At family-owned Jim's Cobbler Concierge in Manhattan, customers last year started bringing in belts by the dozens, said client relations director CJ Burgos — a trend so sweeping that the store has dubbed it "belt-zempic." GLP-1 users are even seeing their feet shrink, Burgos said, prompting an uptick in shoe adjustments. "It's helped the business, but we've also helped clients save," said Burgos, who has also brought in belts to shorten since losing about 60 pounds on Ozempic. SECONDHAND SEIZES THE MOMENT, TOO GLP-1 users are tightening their belts in more ways than one. The drugs' surging popularity in the US is also boosting discount chains, thrift shops and secondhand clothing platforms as many users refrain from splurging on new clothes while their size remains in flux. Compared to other business tailwinds, what sets GLP-1s apart is "the scale and speed," said Alon Rotem, chief strategy officer at online thrift store ThredUp. Shoppers are shifting to smaller sizes, especially when buying jeans: 43% of buyers who started above a waist size 28 are now buying smaller jeans than when they joined ThredUp, Rotem said. Stitch Fix, an online personal styling service, is now offering more adjustable sizing and stretchy fabrics so that people who are rapidly losing weight have the "right apparel to help them bridge multiple sizes," said CEO Matt Baer. He estimated that at least 20% of the company's new clients are on a GLP-1 medication and looking for help finding new sizes. "We've always known that resale and thrift are very popular choices for people in life transition," said Rotem of ThredUp. "As we see that there are many more people in life transition with the advent of GLP-1s, we're leaning into that." item.title: The midterm election outcomes that could shape Trump's final two years
item.description: Americans vote on November 3 in midterm elections that will determine who controls Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term.
item.dc:creator: Tim Reid
item.content:encoded: Americans vote on November 3 in midterm elections that will determine who controls Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's term. Democrats need a net gain of four seats in the US House of Representatives as well as the Senate to overturn Republicans' narrow 218-214 and 53-47 majorities. Opinion polls favor the Democrats to win the House, while the Senate remains too close to call. With Trump's approval rating at the [USN:L6N465159 TEXT:"lowest of his presidency"], the election could reshape Washington. Yet even if Democrats win one or both chambers, Trump would retain veto power and broad executive authority, limiting Democrats' ability to enact major legislation. Analysts, strategists and economists interviewed by Reuters said fights over raising the debt ceiling and government funding are likely in 2027 regardless of the election outcome. Below are the main scenarios and what they could mean for Trump's presidency, Congress and the economy. DEMOCRATS WIN THE HOUSE, NOT THE SENATE Democratic House majority: 5 to 20 seats - Democrats gain control of House committees, subpoena power and the ability to investigate Trump and his administration. - Trump administration officials targeted by congressional subpoenas could defy them because a Justice Department led by Trump appointees is unlikely to enforce them. - Trump retains veto power and broad authority over tariffs, immigration and foreign policy. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on October 20 there would be [USN:S0N431098 TEXT:""very little""] a Democratic-controlled House could do to block Trump's agenda. - Senate Republicans block most Democratic priorities. - Democrats can pass symbolic "messaging" bills on healthcare, abortion rights, housing and AI data centers, but few if any are likely to become law. - Debt ceiling fights, budget battles and government shutdown threats loom in 2027. Impact: Democrats can investigate Trump and his administration through hearings and subpoenas, but not substantially reshape policy. Analysts expect a debt limit showdown by summer that could rattle markets and unsettle investors. Trump, who has largely bypassed Congress over the past two years, is likely to continue advancing his agenda through executive orders. Democratic House majority: 21 to 40 seats - Leadership has more room to absorb defections and advance Democratic priorities. - A larger freshman class, including more progressive members, could increase calls for Trump's [USN:S0N3WW01L TEXT:"impeachment"]. - Some Republicans may be more willing to break with Trump on issues such as tariffs and the Iran war , which opinion polls show are unpopular. - A larger Democratic majority could strengthen Democrats' hand in budget and debt ceiling negotiations, making it easier to win concessions from Republicans. - Democrats have more votes and an easier path to pass bills on healthcare, abortion rights and living costs, forcing difficult votes for Senate Republicans. Impact: Democrats will likely pass bills to signal they want to tackle inflation, curb Trump's war powers and oppose data centers. But major legislative breakthroughs remain unlikely because Senate Republicans can block them and Trump also has veto power. Trump can continue to govern through executive actions, and a debt ceiling fight remains likely. DEMOCRATS WIN THE HOUSE, SENATE SPLITS 50-50 - Republicans keep control of the Senate because Vice President JD Vance can break tie votes. - A handful of senators willing to break with their party, including Pennsylvania Democrat John Fetterman and some moderate Republicans, could become kingmakers on close votes. - Debt ceiling and budget battles become more unpredictable because neither party can afford defections, giving a handful of senators the power to shape or delay a deal. Impact: Washington might be gridlocked with a handful of swing senators determining the outcome of fiscal, judicial and political battles. Trump should be able to win Senate confirmation of nominees with Vance's tie-breaking vote, while his tariff, immigration and foreign policies remain largely unchecked. DEMOCRATS WIN THE HOUSE AND SENATE Senate control may carry greater consequences than House control alone because the chamber determines judicial confirmations, cabinet appointments and ambassadorial nominations. Senate Democratic majority: 2 seats - Democrats take control of Senate committees and the chamber's agenda. - They will likely block many of Trump's judicial nominees and could seek to delay filling any US Supreme Court vacancy until after the 2028 presidential election. - Republicans will likely rush through confirmations before the new Congress is seated in January. - Trump retains veto power and executive authority. Major legislation remains difficult because most bills require 60 votes to overcome a filibuster, a Senate rule that allows the minority party to block or delay legislation. - Control of both chambers gives Democrats more bargaining power in debt ceiling and budget negotiations, although the risk of fiscal standoffs remains significant. Impact: Democrats gain a significant check on Trump's appointments, but narrow margins, the filibuster and Trump's veto limit major legislative gains. Senate Democratic majority: 4 to 6 seats - Leadership is less hostage to individual senators and can afford some defections. - Democrats are more likely to pass bills on tariffs, data centers, healthcare, living costs and limits on presidential war powers and force Trump to veto them. - Those veto fights help Democrats frame the 2028 campaign. - Judicial confirmations largely grind to a halt. Impact: Democrats have a better chance to pass bills that address voter concerns over high prices, healthcare costs and data centers, and increase pressure on Republicans. But Trump still retains the power to block most major legislation. With a bigger majority, voters likely will look to Democrats to address their economic concerns, not just oppose Trump. Trump gains a political foil, allowing him to share blame for Washington's shortcomings and potentially pin economic problems and high prices on Democrats, who he can say are now at the very least equally culpable for the state of the economy. Senate Democratic majority: 8 seats or more - Democrats could claim a clear electoral mandate and argue that voters rebuked Trump's handling of the first half of his second term. - Democrats enter fiscal negotiations with Republicans and the White House over government funding and the debt ceiling from their strongest position, because they have more votes to pass the relevant bills. - Democrats still lack the votes to overcome filibusters, override vetoes or convict Trump in any impeachment trial if House Democrats decide to impeach him. Impact: Democrats gain greater leverage but governing remains constrained by Trump's veto, the filibuster and shared political responsibility for the economy. REPUBLICANS KEEP CONTROL OF BOTH HOUSE AND SENATE While unlikely, given the number of vulnerable House Republicans defending seats, this remains possible. Impact: Trump and Republicans would claim a fresh mandate for his final two years in office. With unified control of Washington, an emboldened Trump would face few congressional constraints and continue advancing judicial nominees and other appointments. The risk of major budget, government shutdown and debt ceiling confrontations would be reduced.

item.content:encoded: Elections législatives en Serbie, l'opposition tente de renverser Vucic BELGRADE, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Serbes se rendent aux urnes dimanche alors que les opposants du dirigeant populiste Aleksandar Vucic, qui a accédé au pouvoir en 2014, l'accusent de corruption. Russie-Trois morts dans des attaques dans la région de Belgorod MOSCOU, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Deux personnes ont été tuées et 13 autres blessées dans la nuit de samedi à dimanche par une attaque de drone ukrainienne contre la ville de Belgorod, en Russie, près de la frontière entre les deux pays, ont déclaré les autorités locales. L'Arabie saoudite intercepte des missiles et des drones 25 octobre (Reuters) - L'Arabie saoudite a intercepté dimanche des drones et des missiles au-dessus de sa capitale Ryad et du sud de son territoire, a dit la coalition emmenée par les Saoudiens contre les Houthis au Yémen. Ouchakov, conseiller de Poutine, prône une implication européenne dans les efforts de paix en Ukraine MOSCOU, 25 octobre (Reuters) - L'Europe doit être impliquée dans les discussions sur une issue au conflit entre l'Ukraine et la Russie car sa position pourrait être déterminante, a déclaré dimanche Iouri Ouchakov, conseiller diplomatique du président russe Vladimir Poutine. Le séisme au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés Le séisme de magnitude 7 survenu au Tibet a fait 16 morts et 65 blessés, a annoncé vendredi le gouvernement local sur les réseaux sociaux. Brésil-Lula et Bolsonaro mobilisent leurs partisans à la veille du second tour de la présidentielle SÃO PAULO, 24 octobre (Reuters) - Le président sortant Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva et le sénateur Flavio Bolsonaro ont clôturé samedi leur campagne en vue du second tour de l'élection présidentielle au Brésil, en mobilisant leurs partisans et en lançant un dernier appel aux électeurs indécis. Election présidentielle en Bulgarie dans un contexte d'attaques en mer Noire SOFIA, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Les Bulgares sont appelés aux urnes dimanche pour une élection présidentielle qui intervient alors que la guerre en Ukraine s'étend au large de la côte bulgare en mer Noire. Environ 1.200 Palestiniens déplacés à Hébron par une opération militaire israélienne JÉRUSALEM, 24 octobre (Reuters) - L'armée israélienne a contraint environ 1.200 Palestiniens à quitter leurs foyers à Hébron, en Cisjordanie occupée, a déclaré samedi un responsable palestinien, au lendemain d'une attaque qui a coûté la vie à deux soldats israéliens. Allemagne-Le "nid d'aigle" des nazis en Bavière incendié Le "nid d'aigle", ancienne résidence des dignitaires du régime nazi dans les montagnes bavaroises du sud de l'Allemagne, a pris feu vendredi soir et un suspect a été arrêté, a annoncé la police allemande. Le dirigeant nord-coréen Kim Jong Un en visite en Chine Le dirigeant de la Corée du Nord Kim Jong Un s'est rendu samedi en Chine en empruntant un pont tout juste ouvert entre les deux pays, a-t-on appris d'un responsable gouvernemental sud-coréen.

item.content:encoded: Le suspect de l'attaque dans les Yvelines placé en observation psychiatrique PARIS, 25 octobre (Reuters) - Le suspect de l'attaque commise vendredi dans les Yvelines, qui a fait un mort et cinq blessés graves, dont une fillette de 12 ans, a été placé en observation psychiatrique, le temps d'apprécier si son état de santé est compatible avec la poursuite des auditions, a annoncé dimanche le parquet national antiterroriste (PNAT). La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque de Trappes prolongée La garde à vue du suspect de l'attaque commise vendredi dans les Yvelines, qui a fait un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fillette de 12 ans, a été prolongée, a annoncé samedi le parquet national antiterroriste (PNAT). Jordan Bardella reconduit à la présidence du Rassemblement national Jordan Bardella a été reconduit samedi à la présidence du Rassemblement national, premier parti d'opposition de France, lors d'un congrès à Orléans (Loiret) où des personnalités de gauche ont participé de leur côté à une manifestation hostile à l'extrême droite. Veillée d'armes avant une nouvelle journée de manifestations, le dispositif sécuritaire renforcé La France se préparait vendredi à une nouvelle journée de manifestations à hauts risques samedi, une semaine après les violences et les pillages survenus en marge de défilés pour les conditions d'enseignement détériorées et contre la vie chère, obligeant l'exécutif à un sursaut. Le Pnat saisi après des tirs dans les Yvelines, sur place Macron dénonce un acte terroriste raciste Le président Emmanuel Macron s'est rendu à Trappes, dans les Yvelines, l'une des communes où un homme à bord d'un véhicule a tiré vendredi à l'arme automatique sur la voie publique, faisant un mort et quatre blessés graves, dont une fille de 12 ans. La tempête Austen balaie l'ouest de la France, 161.000 foyers privés d'électricité Quelque 161.000 foyers étaient privés d'électricité vendredi matin dans l'ouest de la France balayé par la tempête Austen, la première de l'automne, qui s'accompagne de vents violents, rapporte Enedis. Macron annonce l'interdiction des manifestations "sans légitimité" Les autorités interdiront dans les prochains jours les manifestations et regroupements sans "légitimité" et proposeront des "tracés alternatifs" aux syndicats pour protéger les centre-villes, a annoncé jeudi Emmanuel Macron, à deux jours d'un nouvel appel à manifester émanant notamment des "gilets jaunes". France: Premier décès lié au virus Shamonda, aucun risque sanitaire à ce jour selon les autorités Un patient est décédé début octobre du virus de Shamonda, une première en France et dans le monde, a annoncé jeudi le gouvernement, ajoutant qu'il n'y avait à ce stade aucun risque sanitaire pour la population générale au vu des connaissances sur ce virus. Cisjordanie: Les oliveraies de Palestiniens pillées lors d'attaques violentes de colons israéliens Ému aux larmes en se remémorant l'attaque contre son oliveraie par des colons israéliens il y a environ deux semaines près du village palestinien de Lubban al-Gharbi, en Cisjordanie, Ahmed Salem a déclaré s'être retrouvé impuissant, craignant d'être agressé s'il tentait d'intervenir pour protéger son exploitation. Gaza: Trois Palestiniens tués par des frappes israéliennes selon les secours Des frappes et des tirs israéliens ont tué au moins trois Palestiniens jeudi, dans deux incidents séparés survenus dans la bande Gaza, selon les autorités sanitaires locales.
